title: Africa Day: SKWT's Place in the AFR100 Initiative
dek: A continental movement, taking root in Elgeyo Marakwet
body: Each year, Africa Day is a moment to reflect on shared progress across the continent. For Save Kenya Water Towers (SKWT), it is also a moment to recognise the part local, community-rooted work plays in a much larger movement: the African Forest Landscape Restoration Initiative, known as AFR100.
A continental commitment

Launched under an African Union mandate, AFR100 is a country-led effort to bring 100 million hectares of deforested and degraded land across Africa into restoration by 2030. To date, 28 African nations have signed on, together committing more than 113 million hectares to restoration, supported by a network of technical and financial partners including Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ).
SKWT's role on the ground

In Elgeyo Marakwet County, SKWT is helping carry this continental ambition into practice. With support from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and funding from BMZ under AFR100, SKWT is implementing a programme spanning three connected outputs: reviewing the Kipkabus Participatory Forest Management Plan, developing the Spencer Line Management Plan, and supporting community-led restoration through agroforestry and Assisted Natural Regeneration.

Alongside the FAO-supported programme, SKWT has, since 2024, been running a separate restoration effort in Morop location, Keiyo South, funded by the World Resources Institute (WRI) under TerraFund-AFR100. Through a combination of active planting and Assisted Natural Regeneration, the site has grown approximately 99,000 indigenous trees to date.

Each output ties restoration directly to the people who live closest to the land, from county officials and forest associations to farmers and community elders, echoing AFR100's own premise that lasting restoration must be locally led.

The Morop initiative pairs ecological restoration with tangible community benefit. Local households have received 2,000 Hass avocado seedlings to support household income, alongside 40 beehives that supply honey while also discouraging tree-cutting, echoing the same buffer principle behind traditional apiary practice elsewhere in the region. Together, these interventions are aimed at stabilising the landscape while giving communities a direct stake in keeping it standing.
Local work, continental impact

Every hectare restored, whether along the Spencer Line, through the Kipkabus forest, or across the Morop landscape, adds, in a small but real way, to Africa's collective 100-million-hectare target. This Africa Day, SKWT's work across both fronts is a reminder that continental goals are achieved not in the abstract, but through the sustained, patient effort of communities restoring the landscapes they call home.

title: Bees: A Biodiversity Hotspot
dek: How a small insect sustains the whole landscape
body: Of all the creatures that shape a healthy landscape, few work as quietly or as tirelessly as the bee. As they move from flower to flower in search of nectar, bees carry pollen between plants, a simple act that underpins much of the food we eat and the forests we depend on.

It is estimated that bees and other pollinators support the reproduction of a large share of the world's flowering plants, including many of the fruits, vegetables, and crops that communities rely on for food and income. Without them, whole ecosystems would struggle to regenerate.

Bees also indicate the health of a landscape. Where bee populations thrive, it is often a sign of diverse, well-managed vegetation and minimal chemical interference. Where they decline, it can signal degradation, habitat loss, or overuse of pesticides.

In many rural communities, beekeeping has long been more than a livelihood. Hives placed along forest boundaries have traditionally served a dual purpose: supporting pollination while discouraging encroachment and even helping to buffer against wildfire, since bees are known to deter human and animal activity in the areas they occupy.

As landscapes across the region face growing pressure from deforestation and unsustainable land use, protecting pollinators is increasingly recognised as a simple, low-cost way to support both biodiversity and community livelihoods. A single hive, carefully placed, can do far more than produce honey: it can help hold a landscape together.

title: Climate Resilience Farming: What Smallholders Are Teaching Us
dek: Lessons in adaptation, drawn from the land itself
body: 28 Sept 2025

Across Elgeyo Marakwet's escarpments and valleys, it is often the smallest farms that hold the clearest lessons in resilience. Long before climate resilience became a technical term, smallholder farmers were already adapting, diversifying crops, reading rainfall patterns, and shaping their land to withstand a season that might not go as planned.
Diversity as a safety net

Where a single crop can fail with a poor rainy season, a mixed compound rarely fails completely. Farmers along the Spencer Line have long paired avocado and coffee with passion fruit, vegetables, and indigenous trees, a form of agroforestry that spreads risk across the calendar and across the market. When one crop struggles, another often carries the household through.
Sharing what works

Champion farmers play a quiet but critical role in this adaptation. One farmer's success with a coffee nursery or a new fruit variety rarely stays contained to a single compound; cuttings, seedlings, and advice pass from neighbour to neighbour, turning individual experimentation into a shared, community-wide practice.
Working with the land, not against it

Assisted Natural Regeneration and similar practices reflect the same instinct at a landscape scale: rather than imposing a fixed plan on degraded land, they work with what the soil and existing vegetation can already offer, allowing native trees to recover and stabilise the ground around farms and waterways.

As formal climate resilience strategies are developed at the county and national level, smallholders offer a useful reminder: adaptation is rarely a single intervention. It is built, season by season, from diversity, shared knowledge, and a close working relationship with the land.

title: Endangered Species Day: Water, Wildlife, and the Web That Connects Them
dek: Why flora, fauna, and communities all depend on the same source
body: Every living thing in a landscape, plant, animal, and person, is bound together by the same essential need: water. Endangered Species Day is a fitting moment to consider just how deeply flora and fauna depend on one another, and how much of that relationship rests on a resource none of them can do without.
An interconnected system

Forests hold soil in place and regulate rainfall. Wetlands and rivers sustain the plants that animals graze and shelter in. Wildlife, in turn, disperses seeds, pollinates flowers, and keeps vegetation in balance. Remove one part of this system and the rest begins to weaken: degraded forests mean drier rivers, drier rivers mean fewer grazing grounds, and fewer grazing grounds push wildlife into closer contact with people.
Water at the centre

Kenya's water towers, forested highlands like Elgeyo Hills, Mau, and Cherangani, feed the rivers and streams that wildlife and communities alike rely on. When these catchments are degraded, the effects ripple outward: rivers run lower, dry seasons bite harder, and both animals and people are forced to travel further and compete more directly for the water that remains.
Living alongside wildlife

Communities settled along these landscapes have always coexisted with wildlife, often guided by traditional knowledge of migration routes, water points, and seasonal patterns. Protecting flora and fauna, then, is rarely separate from protecting people's own water security and livelihoods. Restoring a forest or a riverbank benefits the elephant, the bee, and the farmer downstream in equal measure.

This Endangered Species Day is a reminder that protecting a single species starts with protecting the water, the forests, and the connections that hold the whole landscape, and everyone in it, together.

title: Farmer Training Day Recap: Agroforestry Techniques That Work
body: Following its inception meeting with local leaders and cooperative officials in Soy North and Soy South, Save Kenya Water Towers (SKWT) has held its first Training of Trainers day, putting agroforestry techniques into farmers' hands.

On 30 April, SKWT trained officials from the Farmer Co-operative Societies at Chepsirei Ward Office, together with the women and youth who turned up as champions, just as encouraged at the earlier meeting. The training covered practical agroforestry techniques for integrating trees into farmland, alongside coffee management and soil and land management practices suited to the area's erosion-prone terrain.

Strong turnout from women and youth across the cooperatives was a highlight of the day, reflecting the emphasis SKWT placed on their participation from the start. Trained representatives are now expected to cascade what they learned to fellow farmers within their cooperatives, extending the reach of the training well beyond those in the room.

SKWT thanks the Soy North and Soy South Farmer Co-operative Societies and Ward Agricultural Officers for their partnership so far, and looks forward to the next steps in bringing agroforestry and assisted natural regeneration to the community.

title: What Is FMNR and Why does it Matter in Restoration Work ?
body: Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) is a low-cost land restoration technique in which farmers regrow trees and shrubs from living stumps, roots and seeds already present in the soil, rather than planting new seedlings. It involves selecting, pruning, thinning and protecting trees that regenerate from re-sprouting rootstock or seeds, restoring vegetation with little to no seedling propagation needed. The practice works by thinning shoots from tree stumps or wild saplings to rapidly foster their growth into mature trees.

The idea was pioneered in Niger in 1983 by Tony Rinaudo, then a young agronomist frustrated by failed tree-planting campaigns. He discovered that what looked like barren farmland was in fact sitting on an “underground forest” of living root systems, capable of resprouting if farmers simply protected and managed the shoots instead of clearing them.
How It Works: The Core Technique
FMNR draws on the centuries-old practice of coppicing and pollarding. The basic steps, as documented across multiple field guides, are consistent:
Survey the land to identify living stumps and self-sown wildings, often small enough to be mistaken for weeds or shrubs.
Select the strongest stems on each stump, typically leaving five or so of the tallest and straightest.
Cull the excess shoots, using the cut material for firewood, and leave the cut leaves on the ground where they suppress erosion and return nutrients to the soil.
Prune the remaining stems roughly halfway up, cutting upward to avoid tearing the bark.
Return every two to six months for follow-up pruning, removing unwanted new growth and side branches to speed up straight, vigorous growth.
Protect the site from uncontrolled grazing and fire until the regrowth is tall enough to withstand browsing.

Farmers are free to adapt density and timing to their own needs. Recommended planting density when intercropped with cereals is commonly cited at 50 to 100 trees per hectare, though this varies by species and purpose. For fruit or timber trees, a single dominant stem is often favoured for faster, straighter growth.
Variants and Related Techniques
FMNR proper – applied on active farmland, integrated directly with crops and grazing.

Assisted Natural Regeneration (ANR) – the broader umbrella term, typically applied on forest land, abandoned land or livestock exclosures rather than farmland under active cultivation. This is the version SKWT is already implementing under Terrafund for AFR100  of its WRI-funded programme, alongside agroforestry.

Intensive FMNR – a more aggressive form where every sprouting stump on a plot is deliberately managed for maximum wood or fruit yield, rather than a lighter-touch approach that leaves some regeneration unmanaged.
Examples from Other Organisations

Niger, where FMNR began, remains the flagship case. Farmer-led regreening restored roughly 200 million trees across 5 million hectares of degraded farmland, with FMNR spreading at a rate of 250,000 hectares per year over two decades. Notably, this happened with minimal government support at the time and, in Rinaudo's account, despite forestry policies that actively discouraged it.

Ethiopia's Humbo project, launched by World Vision in 2006, turned a community-managed reforestation effort into one of the earliest FMNR-based carbon projects. Within a year, communities that had previously had to buy firewood were meeting their own domestic needs and selling surplus wood and hay.

Malawi offers a striking, under-reported case: satellite data uncovered in 2019 revealed large-scale farmer-led regreening had already reached 3.2 million hectares, alongside similar spread in Mali, Chad and Ethiopia.

Kenya is one of World Vision's four designated catalyst countries for scaling FMNR (alongside Ethiopia, Uganda and Zambia), chosen for its combination of degraded and arid land, high poverty levels, and government commitment to restoration. World Vision's Kenya figures put direct FMNR-influenced coverage at roughly 745,000 hectares, with an indirect spread effect covering a further 3.76 million hectares. Kenya has separately committed to restoring 5.1 million hectares under the Bonn Challenge. Closer to home, a WOCAT-documented case from Baringo County (Van Schoubroeck, 2018) found that integrating trees into farming systems reduced the variability of food and fodder production, a direct neighbour to Elgeyo Marakwet's own restoration challenges.
Policy Dimension

FMNR's growth has consistently outpaced the policy environment around it. Land users' rights over trees on their own land are the single biggest enabling factor: laws granting user rights or ownership rights to land users, and laws enabling fair, transparent marketing of FMNR products, tend to increase confidence and uptake of the practice. Where tenure is unclear, farmers have little incentive to protect regrowth they may not be allowed to harvest or sell.

World Vision's current Ethiopia scaling plan illustrates what an enabling policy push looks like in practice: undertaking formal policy review and dialogue forums for dryland restoration, and building coalitions between government, technical partners and community “FMNR champions” through National Alliance and Centre of Expertise platforms. The pattern across catalyst countries is similar: national restoration pledges (Bonn Challenge, UNCCD commitments) create the political opening, but uptake still depends on translating that into secure, farmer-level rights to the trees being managed.
Agriculture Integration
FMNR is deliberately designed to sit inside active farming systems rather than compete with them:
Soil fertility: leaf litter and nutrient cycling from regenerated trees improve soil structure over time, reducing dependence on external inputs.
Microclimate: tree cover buffers crops against wind, heat and evapotranspiration, which supports more stable yields.
Diversified income: farmers gain staggered returns – firewood from year one, saleable branches from year two, and longer-term fruit, fodder or timber – without giving up cropland.

Resilience evidence: following FMNR implementation in Ethiopia, over 80% of surveyed farmers reported reduced on-farm soil erosion, and 74% reported increased soil fertility. In Senegal and Ghana, households practising FMNR reported lower vulnerability to drought and storm damage compared with non-practising neighbours.
Why It's Considered Sustainable
Cost: it requires no nursery, seedlings or planting budget, only labour and a pruning tool most farmers already own, making it accessible to poor and land-constrained households.

Survival rates: because regrowth draws on established root systems rather than young transplants, FMNR trees generally establish faster and survive better than newly planted seedlings, a known weak point of conventional reforestation.

Local ownership: because farmers manage the regrowth on their own land for their own benefit (firewood, fodder, fruit, income), maintenance continues without ongoing donor input, unlike planted trees that are often abandoned once project funding ends.
The SKWT Connection

SKWT's work – agroforestry and Assisted Natural Regeneration across Ngobisi, Soyo and Kipkanao – sits in the same family of practice as FMNR, and the same enabling conditions (secure land access, farmer ownership, low input cost) apply directly to it. Champion farmers such as Mama Miriam on the Spencer Line, an established champion farmer for the avocado agroforestry initiative who also championed her village's move to establish a coffee nursery, exemplify the same farmer-led ownership model that underpins FMNR's success elsewhere – a useful reference point if SKWT wants to frame its own community-led restoration story for donors or a web story audience.

title: Community Tree Nurseries: From Seedling to Sapling
body: Every restored slope starts the same way: a seed, a pot, and a community willing to tend it every day until it is ready for the ground.
1. Pot & sow
2. Water & grow
3. Harden off
4. Transplant

A nursery's real work happens in the quiet, repetitive stretch between sowing and planting. Seeds are sown by hand, one tray at a time, then watered and shaded through weeks of slow, uneven germination. As seedlings strengthen, shade and water are gradually reduced to harden them for the open, often steep ground they are headed for. Only then are they carried out and transplanted alongside ongoing restoration work, each sapling in the ground a small, direct result of a community's daily attention rather than a one-off planting event.

title: Integrated Landscape Management: The Fragile Elgeyo Marakwet Escarpment
body: Drawn from county topographic, land-use and landslide-susceptibility mapping, and the November 2025 Kenya Inter-Agency Rapid Assessment (KIRA)
Elgeyo Marakwet's name comes from the ridge that defines it. That same ridge, the Elgeyo Escarpment, is also the county's most dangerous ground.

The county's shape is unusual: a narrow, elongated corridor wedged between the Uasin Gishu Plateau to the west and the Kerio Valley to the east, split into three topographic zones. The Highlands cover 49% of the county's land area and hold most of its population, fertile soils and reliable rainfall. The Kerio Valley, semi-arid and lower-lying, covers 40%. Between them sits the Escarpment: just 11% of the county's land, but the single most hazardous strip of ground in it.
Highlands 49%
Escarp 11%
Kerio Valley 40%
A century of warning

The instability of the escarpment is not a new discovery. In the early 1900s, colonial officer William Spencer demarcated what became known as the Spencer Line, a safety boundary intended to keep settlement off the most unstable escarpment slopes. More than a century later, that same line is the subject of SKWT's own Spencer Line Management Plan, because the boundary it marked still matters and, in many places, has long since been
-  Spencer Line demarcated as a safety boundary against settlement on unstable slopes
- Recurring landslides across Endo, Kaptarakwa, Kapchelal, Anin, Siroch, Ngopisi, Kaporol, Kasegut, Embobut/Embolot and Emsoo wards
- Repeated major slope failures in the Lagam escarpment area
Oct–Nov 2025
-  Major mudslide crisis at Chesongoch and Moror, Marakwet East; Spencer Line landslides at Chesongoch and Kipkenda over 2024/2025 killed 39 people in total
What the November 2025 assessment found
The Kenya Inter-Agency Rapid Assessment (KIRA), conducted after the Chesongoch and Moror mudslide, put numbers to the damage:
Households affected
Homes destroyed
Lives lost
4 km²
Farmland affected

Beyond the immediate toll, the assessment recorded damage that reaches well past the disaster site itself: destroyed water pipelines and latrines, a mission hospital swept of its equipment, a shopping centre erased, and, in the Kerio River itself, heavy sedimentation and rising turbidity as eroded escarpment soil moved downstream. Debris blocked waterways in places, forming temporary dams that raise the risk of sudden flooding further down the valley. Eighty percent of displaced households told assessors they did not know when they would be able to return home.
Why the escarpment fails

The county's landslide susceptibility mapping weighs five physical factors to predict where slopes are most likely to fail. Slope itself carries the most weight, but land use and land cover is close behind, ahead of soils, rainfall and stream proximity combined:
Factor
Weight
Slope
Land use / land cover
Soils
Rainfall
Streams

That ordering matters for what can actually be done. Nobody can re-grade a 1,800-metre escarpment. But land use, what grows on a slope, how it is farmed, whether tree cover holds the soil together, is the one major factor in this model that a community and a programme like SKWT's can directly change. It is the difference between a hazard map that only tells you where danger lives, and a landscape strategy that can move some of that risk.
A whole-county goal

The escarpment is where the danger is most visible, but SKWT's ambition is not limited to that 11% strip. Our goal is to bring the entire Elgeyo Marakwet County landscape, Highlands, Escarpment and Kerio Valley alike, into improved and productive management, rather than treating each zone, or each project site within it, as a separate problem to be solved on its own.

That is what distinguishes integrated landscape management (ILM) from a conventional project approach. As FAO's own land and water programme frames it, ILM manages the natural resource base and the livelihoods that depend on it together, at the scale of a whole catchment or landscape rather than a single farm or forest block, because the interactions between them, water, soil, forest, farmland, are what actually determine whether a landscape stays productive. The Practical Guide to Integrated Landscape Management, developed by EcoAgriculture Partners and the 1000 Landscapes for 1 Billion People coalition, sets out five elements that recurring ILM efforts around the world tend to share: a durable multi-stakeholder partnership; a shared understanding of the landscape's history, state and trends; a long-term shared vision with concrete targets; coordinated action and investment; and ongoing monitoring and learning.

Applied to Elgeyo Marakwet, that means recognising how the three zones already depend on one another. Forest cover in the Highlands feeds the rivers the Kerio Valley depends on. Escarpment stability protects the homes and roads that connect the two. Valley-floor agriculture and grazing absorb pressure that would otherwise fall on steeper, more fragile ground. Manage any one zone in isolation and the interdependence gets missed; that gap is exactly what a county-wide landscape strategy is meant to close.
Landscape partnership: County government, KFS, NEMA, FAO, University of Eldoret and community structures working as one coalition, not parallel actors.
Shared understanding: The topographic, land-use and landslide-susceptibility mapping behind this brief, held in common rather than siloed by agency.
Vision and planning: The Spencer Line Management Plan and Kipkabus PFMP, each setting a long-term, spatially explicit plan for its part of the landscape.
Taking action: Community-led agroforestry and Assisted Natural Regeneration, translating the plans into work on the ground.
Impact and learning: Survival rates, beneficiary data and progress reporting that feed back into how the strategy adapts.
Where this brief's findings fit

The KIRA report's own long-term recommendations read like a checklist for exactly the kind of work SKWT is already doing on the escarpment: expand community forestry with incentives for maintaining forest cover, scale up ecological restoration of degraded escarpment zones, sustain community awareness and early-warning training, and establish permanent research and monitoring in the escarpment region.

Spencer Line Management Plan: Revisits a century-old settlement boundary with current science and community input, working with the University of Eldoret and county stakeholders to decide, block by block, where the escarpment can be farmed, restored, or left alone.

Assisted Natural Regeneration and agroforestry: On escarpment and margin land, address the land-use factor directly, the one lever in the susceptibility model that responds to community stewardship rather than geology.
Participatory Forest Management: Including the Kipkabus PFMP review, builds the local institutions that make restoration commitments outlast any single project or funding cycle.

None of this undoes the physics of a steep, saturated slope. But the same mapping that shows the escarpment's danger also shows where community-led restoration has real leverage, land use is not the largest factor in the model, but it is the largest one anyone can act on. Scaled up across all three zones under one landscape-wide strategy, rather than confined to the escarpment alone, that is what integrated landscape management is meant to achieve for Elgeyo Marakwet: not a single fix, but an alignment of land-use planning, forest restoration, early warning and community stewardship across the whole county, aimed at the parts of the risk, and the opportunity, that are within reach.

ILM framing adapted from FAO's Land & Water programme and the Practical Guide to Integrated Landscape Management (EcoAgriculture Partners / 1000 Landscapes for 1 Billion People).

title: Why Elgeyo Marakwet's Water Towers Matter Downstream
body: 2 February 2026

Every 2 February, World Wetlands Day turns attention to the rivers, swamps and springs that keep landscapes and livelihoods alive. In Elgeyo Marakwet, that story begins high above the valley floor, in two forest water towers most people downstream will never see.

Elgeyo Marakwet carries the second-largest forest cover of any county in Kenya, and almost all of it sits inside two blocks: the Cherangany Hills in the north, and the forests of the Elgeyo Hills, the escarpment that runs the length of the county and gives it its name. Together they form the water divide that decides where every drop of rain in the county ends up.
One ridge, two river systems

East of the escarpment, rain gathers into the Kerio catchment, feeding the Kerio River and its tributaries, Kerrer, Torok, Chesegon, Embobut, Embomon, Arror, Mong and Kimwarer, down through the Kerio Valley toward Lake Turkana. These same rivers hold real potential for irrigation and hydro-power, and their seasonal wetlands support grazing and farming across the valley floor.

West of the escarpment, a different set of rivers, Moiben, Chepkaitit and Sabor, drains instead into the Lake Victoria basin. Two coastlines, two countries' worth of downstream users, and both depend on the same forested ridge to hold water back long enough to release it slowly rather than all at once.

Why this matters beyond the county line

Wetlands and rivers rarely respect administrative boundaries, and Elgeyo Marakwet's do not either. What happens on the slopes of the Cherangany Hills and the Elgeyo Escarpment, whether forest cover holds or degrades, decides how much water reaches farms, wetlands and hydro-power potential in the Kerio Valley, and how steadily rivers feed the Lake Victoria basin on the other side of the ridge. Protecting these two water towers is, in a very literal sense, downstream protection for two entirely different drainage systems at once.

This is the case SKWT makes on World Wetlands Day: that community stewardship on a single forested ridge in Elgeyo Marakwet carries consequences for river systems, wetlands and communities far beyond it.

title: Charting a Path for the Spencer Line
dek: SKWT secures high-level buy-in for landscape restoration
body: The Spencer Line escarpment, home to an estimated 50,000 households along the western edge of the Great Rift Valley, has long sustained the communities of Elgeyo Marakwet County. But deforestation, unsustainable farming, and encroachment have taken their toll, a toll made painfully clear by the landslides that struck Chesongoch and Kipkenda in late 2025.

In response, Save Kenya Water Towers (SKWT), with support from FAO under the AFR100 Landscape Restoration Initiative, is developing the Spencer Line Management Plan (SLMP), part of a wider community-led restoration programme for the escarpment. Before any fieldwork could begin, SKWT set out to earn shared ownership of the process.
Opening the conversation

In April 2026, SKWT met with Governor H.E. Wisley Rotich and county leadership to introduce the programme. The Governor welcomed the initiative and directed county departments to lend their full support. A parallel meeting with County Commissioner David Koskei secured national government backing, with Deputy County Commissioner Herbert A. Kombo appointed as SKWT's liaison.

It was in these early conversations that county leaders raised a point that would shape everything to follow: Kerio Valley, now recognised as its own subcounty, sits at the heart of the Spencer Line and needed to be part of the process from the start.
Bringing institutions together

SKWT then convened county departments and national agencies, among them the Kenya Forest Service, NEMA, and the Kenya Red Cross, to map out roles and agree a shared workplan. Stakeholders reviewed and approved the methodology, nominated focal persons, and echoed the call to fully include Kerio Valley given its exposure to landslide risk.

These early steps built something the technical work alone could not: a coordinated platform, owned by county government, national agencies, and community leadership together. With that foundation in place, attention now turns to the communities who call the Spencer Line home, whose knowledge and priorities will shape the plan ahead.

title: New Year, New Season: SKWT's 2026 Restoration Goals
body: 5 January 2026

The new year opened not with fanfare, but with a familiar SKWT ritual: the team gathered to take stock, plan ahead, and recommit to the work of restoring Kenya's water towers. Across the organisation, from field officers to technical leads, the mood was one of quiet resolve. The past year had tested the team, it strengthened something harder to measure: a shared belief that the work matters, and that it belongs to the communities it serves.

Team morale going into 2026 rests on that belief. SKWT's staff have grown into their roles not just as conservationists, but as facilitators, people who spend as much time listening in barazas and focus group discussions, workshops, capacity training as they do walking restoration sites. That shift, from delivering interventions to building genuine local ownership, is central to how the organisation defines success this year.

Partnerships are a second pillar of the 2026 goals. SKWT enters the year continuing its work with WRI – Terrafund for AFR100 while also reaching beyond existing relationships, applying to new support, exploring collaborations like the “Bees for Biodiversity” concept rooted in indigenous Keiyo practice, and strengthening ties with institutions such as the University of Eldoret. Not every application succeeds, but each one sharpens the organisation's case for why community-led restoration deserves investment.

On policy, SKWT is working to ensure that policies are not just documents, but living tools that communities understand and use to assert their stewardship. The goal is influence that outlasts any single project cycle: local institutions equipped to manage their resources, land and forests long after external funding ends.

Implementation in 2026 means translating all of this, morale, partnerships, policy, into visible change on the ground: seedlings that survive, agreements that hold, and communities that see the forest as theirs to protect, not something managed on their behalf. Awareness and ownership are not separate goals from restoration; they are how restoration lasts.
SKWT begins the year clear-eyed about the challenges ahead, and just as clear about why the work continues.

title: What Is Assisted Natural Regeneration (ANR), Where It Applies, and Why It's Cheaper Than Planting
body: 26 January 2026

Kenya's water towers, the Mau Forest Complex, Aberdares, Mt Kenya, Mt Elgon, Elgeyo Hills and the Cherangany Hills, are the country's rain-makers and river-sources, feeding the catchments that supply water, hydropower and agriculture far beyond their boundaries. When their forest cover thins, the effect is not just fewer trees; it is drier rivers, eroded slopes, and a slower, weaker water cycle for everyone downstream. Restoring that cover quickly and at scale is one of the central challenges of landscape restoration in Kenya, and Assisted Natural Regeneration, or ANR, is one of the most practical tools available for the job.

ANR works from a simple observation: degraded land inside and around a water tower is rarely empty. Beneath grass, bracken and bare patches, root stock, stumps and seed banks often survive from the forest that once stood there, waiting for the chance to grow again. Rather than clearing that land and planting new seedlings row by row, ANR protects and encourages what is already there, fencing off grazing, controlling fire, clearing competing weeds, and letting natural regrowth resume, sometimes helped along by pruning or coppicing.

Where it applies matters for ecosystem health as much as for tree cover. ANR is best suited to the degraded, not deforested, land found at forest margins, on overgrazed hillslopes, along riverine buffers, and on fallow land bordering gazetted forest, exactly the transition zones common around water towers like the Cherangany Hills and the Mau. These are the areas where root systems and seed banks usually persist, and where regeneration can restore not just tree cover but the soil structure, water infiltration and streambank stability that keep a catchment functioning. On riverine buffers in particular, ANR can rebuild the vegetation that slows runoff, filters sediment before it reaches a stream, and stabilises banks against erosion, work with a direct line to water quality and flow downstream. ANR is less suited to land converted long-term to other uses, where little natural stock remains to regenerate from; in those areas, planting stays the better option.

The cost argument is where ANR earns its place in a water tower restoration strategy. Raising and transplanting seedlings takes labour, water, potting material and time before a single tree touches degraded ground, and transplant losses can be significant on the steep, exposed slopes typical of highland catchments. ANR skips most of that. There is no seedling to grow, carry uphill or replace if it fails. The intervention is protection and patience, keeping livestock and fire out long enough for existing root systems to resume growth. For restoration work spread across large, difficult-to-reach catchment areas, that difference in cost and effort allows a given budget to cover far more ground, an important consideration when the goal is landscape-scale ecosystem recovery, not just isolated planting sites.

None of this makes ANR effortless. It depends on communities living around the water tower changing behaviour: restraining grazing, respecting fire breaks, and watching over land that, at first, looks like nothing is happening. Local ownership is what turns regenerating stumps into a restored hillside rather than a broken agreement. Applied well across Kenya's water towers, ANR offers a route back to ecosystem health that is not only cheaper than planting, but built on the kind of community stewardship that keeps a catchment protected long after the restoration project ends.

title: World Environment Day Special: Celebrating at Cheptebo
dek: SKWT joins Elgeyo Marakwet County in marking World Environment Day 2026
body: This year's World Environment Day, marked globally on 5 June under the theme "Inspired by Nature. For Climate. For Our Future," was celebrated in Elgeyo Marakwet County at AIC Cheptebo. Save Kenya Water Towers (SKWT) was honoured to be invited as a partner in the celebration, joining county institutions and fellow conservation actors in marking the day.
A tour of Cheptebo's model farm

As a hosting partner, SKWT toured the various institutions within AIC Cheptebo, beginning with its fruit orchards. Rows of mango trees stood alongside avocado, grapes, and pixie citrus, a striking demonstration of what diversified, well-managed agriculture can look like on a single site.

The visit continued through the vegetable garden and on to the fruit processing factory, before taking in the dairy unit and its milk processing plant, facilities that double as a practical training ground for students of the Cheptebo Agricultural Technical Institute.
A shared platform
SKWT took the opportunity to express its support for advancing nature-based solutions in the county, and to introduce its FAO-supported programme to fellow partners and stakeholders present.

The celebration brought together a wide range of institutions, including the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA), the Elgeyo Marakwet County Assembly, the County's Environment and Land Court, Scope Intervention, and students from the Institute. Their presence reflected the collaborative spirit at the heart of this year's theme, bringing government, conservation partners, and the next generation of agricultural practitioners together on common ground.

For SKWT, the day was a chance to see, in practical form, the kind of nature-based, community-rooted approach that underpins its own restoration work across the county's water towers, and a reminder that environmental stewardship and agricultural livelihoods can, and do, grow side by side.
